extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of constitutional theory, citizens interested in governance, and scholars of American political thought
extracted.subtask_description: An analytical essay (Federalist No. 47) arguing principles and practical requirements for separation of powers and checks and balances in republican government. It evaluates constitutional structure, identifies threats (especially legislative encroachment), and recommends safeguards drawn from state experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Departments should be connected to allow constitutional control
rubrics_metrics.description: The Legislative, Executive, and Judiciary departments should not be wholly unconnected; they must be 'so far connected and blended, as to give to each a constitutional control over the others.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Madison argues that some degree of connection is necessary so that each department can check the others in practice; theoretical, absolute separation would prevent practical security against encroachment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Powers of one department must not be directly administered by others
rubrics_metrics.description: The powers properly belonging to one department 'ought not to be directly and completely administered by either of the other departments,' and none ought to possess an 'overruling influence' over the others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This sets a baseline prohibiting direct administration of another branch's core functions and warns against indirect domination or overruling influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical security (checks) required beyond parchment barriers
rubrics_metrics.description: Precisely marking constitutional boundaries ('parchment barriers') is insufficient; experience shows their efficacy is overrated and more adequate defenses are indispensably necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitutions must provide practical mechanisms (controls, checks, dependencies addressed) rather than rely only on written demarcations to prevent encroachment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative department is the principal threat of encroachment
rubrics_metrics.description: In a representative republic the Legislative department (not the Executive) is the greatest source of danger because it has extensive, less-precisely-limited powers and can mask encroachments under complicated or indirect measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Madison explains why legislature's scope, access to public funds, and influence over appointments/salaries make it especially likely to aggrandize power; safeguards should be especially attentive to legislative tendencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: No person should exercise powers of more than one department
rubrics_metrics.description: Separation requires that 'no person should exercise the powers of more than one [department] at the same time.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citing Jefferson: concentrating legislative, executive, and judicial powers even in many hands produces 'elective despotism.' Preventing overlap of office-holding is a key anti-concentration rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divide and balance powers among several bodies to prevent elective despotism
rubrics_metrics.description: Government should be founded on free principles where 'the powers of Government should be so divided and balanced among several bodies of magistracy, as that no one could transcend their legal limits, without being effectually checked and restrained by the others.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The remedy to tyranny is balance among bodies that can check one another; arrangements must make transcending legal limits practically difficult and reliably checked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid dependence of Judiciary and Executive on the Legislature for offices/salaries
rubrics_metrics.description: The Judiciary and Executive were left dependent on the Legislature for their subsistence in office and, in some cases, continuance in it; such dependence enables legislative usurpation because opposition is unlikely or ineffectual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secure tenure and financial independence (or constitutionally fixed compensation) reduce susceptibility to legislative pressure and make effective opposition to encroachment more likely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require prior printing of public bills for popular consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: A constitutional precaution relied upon is that 'all bills of a public nature shall be previously printed for the consideration of the People.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Madison cites the Council of Censors' findings that failure to print bills facilitated improper legislative acts; prior publication increases transparency and public scrutiny, acting as a check.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect trial by jury and prevent legislative intrusion into judicial matters
rubrics_metrics.description: The constitutional trial by jury had been violated and powers not delegated by the Constitution were assumed by the Legislature; preserving jury trials and keeping judicial matters within judiciary competence is essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislative determination of judicial rights and causes undermines separation; safeguards should keep judiciary functions within the judicial sphere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fix judicial salaries to prevent legislative manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: The Constitution expressly requires judicial salaries to be fixed; varying them episodically (by the Legislature) undermines judicial independence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Madison notes instances where salaries were varied and that such practices enable legislative control over judges; constitutionally protected compensation supports impartial adjudication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure the Executive to maintain individual responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: An Executive administered by a single hand (or few hands) is preferable; an Executive composed of many members is akin to a Legislative assembly and lacks individual responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Madison argues Pennsylvania's multi-member Executive resembled a legislature and, being exempt from individual responsibility, was more prone to unauthorized measures. Executive design should favor accountability and restraint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider exceptional contexts (war, congressional recommendation) but treat most encroachments as systemic
rubrics_metrics.description: Some breaches of constitutionality may be produced by necessities of war or recommended by Congress or reflect conformity to legislative sentiment, but the greater part are 'spontaneous shoots of an ill-constituted Government.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing violations, distinguish between exceptional exigencies and normal, avoidable encroachments; do not excuse routine overreach as emergency necessity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power tends to encroach and must be effectually restrained
rubrics_metrics.description: Power is of an encroaching nature, and it 'ought to be effectually restrained from passing the limits assigned to it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This general precaution underlies all specific safeguards: institutional designs must assume ambition and craft restraints that operate in practice, not only on paper.
